metadata.title: Learning Local Image Descriptors with Deep Siamese and Triplet Convolutional Networks by Minimizing Global Loss Functions

extraction_notes.note: Gradient formulas are stated as derived without a shown derivation; emitted as semi_formal claims (equation-only alternative) so the unnumbered display in ClP1 is kept.
The four proposed models are named configurations (network + loss), typed definition rather than algorithm since no procedure is given.
ConvNet architecture strings, the block notation B/P/C, the toy-problem protocol, SGD training settings and the results tables were not made nodes: experimental details not referenced by any node.

nodes.name: Squared Mahalanobis distance
nodes.statement: d_{\mathbf{W}} = (\mathbf{\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j})^\top \mathbf{W} (\mathbf{\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j}),
nodes.statement_short: Squared Mahalanobis distance with matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Jain et al. 2012; Weinberger et al. 2005
nodes.label: eq:linear_DML

nodes.name: Deep ConvNet as layer composition
nodes.statement: f(\mathbf{x},\theta_f) = f_{\text{out}} \circ r_{L} \circ h_L \circ f_L \circ ... \circ r_1 \circ h_1 \circ f_1(\mathbf{x}),
nodes.statement_short: A deep ConvNet is a composition of linear pre-activations, normalisations and nonlinear activations over $L$ layers.
nodes.label: eq:def_CNN

nodes.name: Siamese pairwise (embedding) loss $J_1^s$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} J_1^s( \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j, & \theta_f ) = \delta(y_i-y_j)\| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}_i, \theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}_j, \theta_f) \|_2 - \\ & (1 - \delta(y_i-y_j))\| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}_i, \theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}_j, \theta_f) \|_2, \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Contrastive pairwise loss: distance for same-class pairs minus distance for different-class pairs.
nodes.origin_citation: Chopra et al. 2005; Masci et al. 2014
nodes.label: eq:loss_siamese_embedding

nodes.name: Siamese pairwise similarity loss $J_2^s$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} J_2^s( \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g ) = & \delta(y_i-y_j) (1/(\kappa+g(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g ) )) \\ &+(1 - \delta(y_i-y_j))g(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g ) , \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Similarity loss: inverse similarity for matching pairs plus similarity for non-matching pairs.
nodes.label: eq:loss_siamese_classifier

nodes.name: Triplet loss $J_1^t$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} J_1^t & ( \mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-, \theta_f ) = \\ & \max \left ( 0,1-\frac{ \| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}, \theta_f) - f^{(3)}(\mathbf{x}^-, \theta_f) \|_2 } { \| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}, \theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}^+, \theta_f) \|_2 + m } \right ), \\ \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Ratio-based hinge triplet loss with margin $m$.
nodes.origin_citation: Wang et al. 2014; Hoffer & Ailon; Schroff et al. 2015; Wohlhart & Lepetit 2015
nodes.label: eq:loss_triplet_embedding

nodes.name: Global loss (embedding) $J_1^g$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} J_1^g( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N ,& \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N , \theta_f ) = \\ &(\sigma^{2+}+\sigma^{2-})+\lambda \max\big(0,\mu^+ - \mu^- + t\big), \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Sum of matching/non-matching distance variances plus a hinge on the gap between their means.
nodes.label: eq:loss_global

nodes.name: Gradient of the global loss w.r.t. matching and non-matching embeddings
nodes.statement: \footnotesize{ \begin{split} \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i^+)} = -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^+ - &\mu^+)(f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^+)) \\ &+ \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i ) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^+))\mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big],\\ \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)} = -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^- - &\mu^-)(f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)) \\ &+ \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i^-) - f(\mathbf{x}_i))\mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big]\\ \end{split}}
nodes.statement_short: Gradients of $J_1^g$ with respect to the positive and negative embeddings.
nodes.label: eq:loss_global_gradient

nodes.name: Global loss (pairwise similarity) $J_2^g$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} J_2^g = ( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N ,& \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N , \theta_f ) = \\ &(\sigma^{2+}+\sigma^{2-})+\lambda \max\big(0, m - (\mu^+ - \mu^-) \big),\\ \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Sum of similarity variances plus a hinge on the margin between matching and non-matching mean similarities.
nodes.label: eq:loss_global_siamese

nodes.name: Gradient of the pairwise similarity global loss
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \frac{\partial J_2^g}{\partial g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g)} = \frac{2}{N}\big[ & (g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g) -\mu^+)\\&-\frac{1}{2}\mathds{1}((\mu^+ -\mu^-) < m)\big]\\ \frac{\partial J_2^g}{\partial g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g)} = \frac{2}{N}\big[& (g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g) -\mu^-)\\&+\frac{1}{2}\mathds{1}((\mu^+ -\mu^-) < m)\big].\\ \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Gradients of $J_2^g$ with respect to the matching and non-matching similarity scores.
nodes.label: eq:loss_global_siamese_gradient

nodes.name: Combined triplet and global loss $J_1^{tg}$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &J_1^{tg}( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N , \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N ) = \\ & \gamma \sum_j J_1^t ( \mathbf{x}_j,\mathbf{x}_j^+, \mathbf{x}_j^-) + J_1^g( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N , \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N ),\\ \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Weighted sum of per-triplet triplet losses plus the global loss.
nodes.label: eq:loss_combined

nodes.name: Metric learning
nodes.statement: In general, metric learning (see Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}-(a)) assumes the existence of a set of points represented by $\{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N$, with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb R^n$ and a respective set of labels $\{ y_i \}_{i=1}^N$, with $y_i \in \{1,...,C\}$, and the goal is to find a Mahalanobis distance with parameter $\mathbf{W}$.
differentia: assumes the existence of a set of points represented by $\{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N$, with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb R^n$ and a respective set of labels $\{ y_i \}_{i=1}^N$, with $y_i \in \{1,...,C\}$
the goal is to find a Mahalanobis distance with parameter $\mathbf{W}$
nodes.statement_short: Given labelled points $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb R^n$ with labels $y_i$, find a Mahalanobis distance parameterised by $\mathbf{W}$.

nodes.name: Linear discriminant metric learning (generalised eigenvalue) problem
nodes.statement: For example, the square distance between $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{x}_j$ is~\cite{jain2012metric,weinberger2005distance}: \begin{equation} d_{\mathbf{W}} = (\mathbf{\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j})^\top \mathbf{W} (\mathbf{\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j}), \end{equation} where the factorisation of the matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^\top$ (with $\mathbf{G} \in \mathbb R^{n \times m}$) allows us to formulate the following optimisation problem: $\mathbf{G}^* = \arg \max_{\mathbf{G}} \text{tr} \left ( (\mathbf{G}^\top \mathbf{S}_w \mathbf{G})^{-1} (\mathbf{G}^\top \mathbf{S}_b \mathbf{G}) \right ) $, with $ \mathbf{S}_k = \sum_{ij} \mathbf{Y}_k (\mathbf{\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j})(\mathbf{\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j})^\top$, $\mathbf{Y}_w = \mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Y}_b = 1 - \mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Y}_{ij}=1$ if $y_i=y_j$ and $\mathbf{Y}_{ij}=0$, otherwise.
nodes.origin_citation: Jain et al. 2012; Weinberger et al. 2005
nodes.statement_short: With $\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^\top$, maximise the trace ratio of between-class to within-class scatter projected by $\mathbf{G}$.

nodes.name: Labelled training set of image patches
nodes.statement: As mentioned above in Sec.~\ref{sec:metric_learning}, we assume the existence of a training set of image patches and their respective classes, \ie, $\{ (\mathbf{x}_i,y_i) \}_{i=1}^N$, with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb R^n$ and $y_i \in \{1,...,C\}$ (note that we use $n$ as the patch size to simplify the notation, but the extension to a matrix representation for $\mathbf{x}$ is trivial).
nodes.statement_short: A training set of $N$ labelled patches $(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)$ with $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb R^n$, $y_i\in\{1,\dots,C\}$ is given.

nodes.name: Feature embedding $f(\mathbf{x},\theta_f)$
nodes.statement: The first goal of our work is to use a triplet network and respective triplet loss (defined below in detail)~\cite{Wangcvpr14,hoffer2014deep,SchroffKPcvpr15,wohlhartcvpr15} to produce a feature embedding $f(\mathbf{x},\theta_f)$ defined by $f: \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \rightarrow \mathbb R^m$, where $\theta_f \in \mathbb R^k$ denotes the network parameters (weights, biases and etc.).
nodes.statement_short: The feature embedding is a map $f:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m$ with network parameters $\theta_f$.

nodes.name: Pairwise similarity estimator $g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j,\theta_g)$
nodes.statement: Essentially, the siamese network can form a feature embedding, like the one above, or a pairwise similarity estimator, represented with $g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j , \theta_g)$, which is defined by $g: \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \rightarrow \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: A pairwise similarity estimator is a map $g:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R$.

nodes.name: Siamese network
nodes.statement: The siamese network~\cite{bromley1993signature,Han_cvpr15,masci2014descriptor,ZagoruykoCVPR15} is trained with a two-tower deep ConvNet (Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}-(b)), where the weights on both towers are initialised at the same values and during stochastic gradient descent, they receive the same gradients (\ie, the weights on both towers are tied).
differentia: the weights on both towers are initialised at the same values and during stochastic gradient descent, they receive the same gradients

nodes.name: Deep ConvNet
nodes.statement: We consider the following definition of a deep ConvNet: \begin{equation} f(\mathbf{x},\theta_f) = f_{\text{out}} \circ r_{L} \circ h_L \circ f_L \circ ... \circ r_1 \circ h_1 \circ f_1(\mathbf{x}), \end{equation} where the parameter $\theta_f$ is formed by the network weight matrices, bias vectors, and normalisation parameters for each layer $l \in \{1,...,L\}$, $f_l(.)$ represents the pre-activation function (\ie, the linear transforms in the convolutional layers), $h_l(.)$ represents a normalisation function, and $r_l(.)$ is a non-linear activation function (e.g., ReLU~\cite{nair2010rectified}).
nodes.statement_short: A deep ConvNet composes per-layer pre-activations $f_l$, normalisations $h_l$ and activations $r_l$, followed by an output layer.

nodes.name: Pairwise loss
nodes.statement: A siamese network is then represented by two identical deep ConvNets trained using pairs of labelled inputs, where one possible loss function (called pairwise loss) minimises the distance between embedded features of the same class and maximises the distance between embedded features of different classes, as follows~\cite{chopra2005learning,masci2014descriptor}: \begin{equation} \begin{split} J_1^s( \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j, & \theta_f ) = \delta(y_i-y_j)\| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}_i, \theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}_j, \theta_f) \|_2 - \\ & (1 - \delta(y_i-y_j))\| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}_i, \theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}_j, \theta_f) \|_2, \end{split} \end{equation} where $\delta(.)$ is the Dirac delta function and $f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x},\theta_f)$ is constrained to equal to $f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x},\theta_f)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Chopra et al. 2005; Masci et al. 2014
differentia: minimises the distance between embedded features of the same class and maximises the distance between embedded features of different classes
nodes.statement_short: Siamese pairwise loss: pull same-class embeddings together and push different-class embeddings apart.

nodes.name: Pairwise similarity loss
nodes.statement: Alternatively, the siamese network can be trained as a pairwise similarity estimator, with a pairwise similarity loss that can be defined as: \begin{equation} \begin{split} J_2^s( \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g ) = & \delta(y_i-y_j) (1/(\kappa+g(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g ) )) \\ &+(1 - \delta(y_i-y_j))g(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g ) , \end{split} \end{equation} where the ConvNet $g(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j, \theta_g)$ returns the similarity between the descriptors $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{x}_j$, with $\kappa$ representing a small positive constant.
nodes.statement_short: Loss for a siamese similarity estimator $g$: $1/(\kappa+g)$ on matching pairs, $g$ on non-matching pairs.

nodes.name: Central-surround two-stream network
nodes.statement: It is important to emphasise that the local descriptor learning model that currently produces the smallest error on the UBC dataset (Central-surround two-stream network) consists of a siamese network, trained with a loss similar to (\ref{eq:loss_siamese_classifier}), where the input patch is sampled twice at half the resolution of the input image: one sample containing the whole patch is input to the surround stream and another sample containing a sub-patch at the centre of the original patch is input to the central stream ~\cite{ZagoruykoCVPR15}. The output of these two streams are combined to obtain a similarity score.
nodes.statement_short: A siamese similarity network whose surround stream sees the downsampled whole patch and central stream sees the centre sub-patch.

nodes.name: Triplet network and triplet loss
nodes.statement: The triplet network~\cite{Wangcvpr14,hoffer2014deep,SchroffKPcvpr15,wohlhartcvpr15} (Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}-(d)) is an extension of the siamese network that is trained with triplets at the input (which produces an embedding) using the triplet loss function, as follows: \begin{equation} \begin{split} J_1^t & ( \mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-, \theta_f ) = \\ & \max \left ( 0,1-\frac{ \| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}, \theta_f) - f^{(3)}(\mathbf{x}^-, \theta_f) \|_2 } { \| f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}, \theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}^+, \theta_f) \|_2 + m } \right ), \\ \end{split} \end{equation} where $m$ is the margin, $\mathbf{x}^+$ and $\mathbf{x}$ belong to the same class, $\mathbf{x}^-$ and $\mathbf{x}$ are from different classes, and $f^{(1)}(.)$, $f^{(2)}(.)$ and $f^{(3)}(.)$ are constrained to be the same network.
nodes.origin_citation: Wang et al. 2014; Hoffer & Ailon; Schroff et al. 2015; Wohlhart & Lepetit 2015
differentia: trained with triplets at the input (which produces an embedding) using the triplet loss function
nodes.statement_short: Triplet network: three tied towers trained on (anchor, positive, negative) triplets with a ratio-based hinge loss of margin $m$.

nodes.name: Triplet loss versus pairwise loss
nodes.statement: Note that the losses in (\ref{eq:loss_siamese_embedding}) and (\ref{eq:loss_triplet_embedding}) are apparently similar, but they have a noticeable difference, which is the fact that a triplet of similar and dissimilar inputs gives context for the optimisation process, as opposed to the pairwise loss that the siamese network minimises (same class) or maximises (different classes) as much as possible for each pair independently~\cite{hoffer2014deep}.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the pairwise loss, the triplet loss gives relative context to the optimisation.

nodes.name: Matching and non-matching distances follow two distinct distributions
nodes.statement: The main idea behind our proposed loss function is the avoidance of the over- or under-sampling problems mentioned above with the assumption that the distances (or similarities) between descriptors of the same class (i.e., matching pairs) or different classes (i.e., non-matching pairs) are samples from two distinct distributions.
nodes.statement_short: Distances (or similarities) of matching and non-matching pairs are samples from two distinct distributions.

nodes.name: Global loss function (feature embedding)
nodes.statement: Fig.~\ref{fig:global_loss}-(a) depicts the reasoning behind the design of the proposed global loss function, which is defined for the feature embedding case by: \begin{equation} \begin{split} J_1^g( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N ,& \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N , \theta_f ) = \\ &(\sigma^{2+}+\sigma^{2-})+\lambda \max\big(0,\mu^+ - \mu^- + t\big), \end{split} \end{equation} where $\mu^+ = \sum_{i=1}^N d_i^+/N,~~ \mu^- = \sum_{i=1}^N d_i^-/N $, ~~ $\sigma^{2+} = \sum_{i=1}^N(d_i^+ -\mu^+)^2/N,~~~ \sigma^{2-} = \sum_{i=1}^N(d_i^- - \mu^-)^2/N$, with $\mu^+$ and $\sigma^{2+}$ denoting the mean and variance of the matching pair distance distribution, $\mu^-$ and $\sigma^{2-}$ representing the mean and variance of the non-matching pair distance distribution, $d_i^+ = \frac{\lVert f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}_i,\theta_f) - f^{(2)}(\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_f) \rVert_2^2}{4}$, $d_i^- = \frac{\lVert f^{(1)}(\mathbf{x}_i,\theta_f) - f^{(3)}(\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_f) \rVert_2^2}{4}$, $\lambda$ is a term that balances the importance of each term, $t$ is the margin between the mean of the matching and non-matching distance distributions and $N$ is the size of the training set.
nodes.statement_short: Global embedding loss: variances of matching and non-matching distances plus a hinge forcing a margin $t$ between their means.

nodes.name: Normalised distances lie in [0,1]
nodes.statement: Note in (\ref{eq:loss_global}), that we assume a triplet network (i.e., $f^{(1)}(.)$, $f^{(2)}(.)$ and $f^{(3)}(.)$ are the same network), where the squared Euclidean distances of the matching and non-matching pairs of the $i^{th}$ triplet are constrained to be $0 \leq d_i^+, d_i^- \leq 1$ because of the division by 4, and the normalisation layer enforces that the norm of the embedding is 1.
nodes.statement_short: With unit-norm embeddings and division by 4, matching and non-matching distances lie in $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Gradient of the global loss $J_1^g$
nodes.statement: Given that we use SGD for the optimisation process, we need to derive the gradient of the global loss function, as follows: \begin{equation*} \footnotesize{ \begin{split} \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i)} &= -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^+ - \mu^+)\big(f(\mathbf{x}_i^+) - f(\mathbf{x}_i)\big)+ 2(d_i^- - \mu^-)\\ &\big(f(\mathbf{x}_i^-) - f(\mathbf{x}_i)\big) + \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i^+) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)) \mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big],\\ \end{split}} \end{equation*} \begin{equation} \footnotesize{ \begin{split} \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i^+)} = -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^+ - &\mu^+)(f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^+)) \\ &+ \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i ) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^+))\mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big],\\ \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)} = -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^- - &\mu^-)(f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)) \\ &+ \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i^-) - f(\mathbf{x}_i))\mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big]\\ \end{split}} \end{equation} where the dependence on $\theta_f$ and the channel index $f^{(.)}$ are dropped to simplify the notation, and $\mathds{1}(a)$ is an indicator function with value $1$ when $a$ is true.
conclusions: \footnotesize{ \begin{split} \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i^+)} = -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^+ - &\mu^+)(f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^+)) \\ &+ \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i ) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^+))\mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big],\\ \frac {\partial J_1^g}{\partial f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)} = -\frac{1}{2N}\Big[2(d_i^- - &\mu^-)(f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)) \\ &+ \lambda (f(\mathbf{x}_i^-) - f(\mathbf{x}_i))\mathds{1}((\mu^- - \mu^+) < t) \Big]\\ \end{split}}
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form gradients of the global loss $J_1^g$ with respect to anchor, positive and negative embeddings.

nodes.name: Global loss gradient depends on whole-training-set statistics
nodes.statement: It is important to note that the gradient ${\partial J_1^t}{/ \partial f(\mathbf{x}_i)}$ of the triplet loss in (\ref{eq:loss_triplet_embedding}) depends only on the $i^{th}$ triplet of the training set, whereas the gradient ${\partial J_1^g}{/ \partial f(\mathbf{x}_i)} $ of the global loss in (\ref{eq:loss_global_gradient}) depends on $\mu^+$ and $\mu^-$, which in turn depends on the statistics of the samples in the whole training set. This dependence on global training set statistics has the potential to suppress the spurious gradients computed from outliers and thus improving the generalisation of the trained model.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the triplet loss gradient, the global loss gradient depends on training-set means, which may suppress outlier gradients.

nodes.name: Global loss function (pairwise similarity)
nodes.statement: Fig.~\ref{fig:global_loss}-(b) shows the idea behind the design of the proposed pairwise similarity global loss function, which is defined by: \begin{equation} \begin{split} J_2^g = ( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N ,& \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N , \theta_f ) = \\ &(\sigma^{2+}+\sigma^{2-})+\lambda \max\big(0, m - (\mu^+ - \mu^-) \big),\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where $g(\mathbf{x},\tilde{\mathbf{x}},\theta_g)$ produces a similarity score between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, $\mu^+ = \sum_{i=1}^N g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g)/N,~~ \mu^- = \sum_{i=1}^N g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g)/N $, ~~ $\sigma^{2+} = \sum_{i=1}^N(g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+) -\mu^+)^2/N,~~~ \sigma^{2-} = \sum_{i=1}^N(g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-) - \mu^-)^2/N$, with $\mu^+$ and $\sigma^{2+}$ denoting the mean and variance of the matching pair similarity distribution, $\mu^-$ and $\sigma^{2-}$ representing the mean and variance of the non-matching pair similarity distribution, $\lambda$ is a term that balances the importance of each term, $m$ is the margin between the mean of the matching and non-matching similarity distributions and $N$ is again the size of the training set (note that we are abusing the notation with the re-definition of $\mu^+$, $\mu^-$, $\sigma^{2+}$, and $\sigma^{2-}$).
nodes.statement_short: Global similarity loss: variances of matching and non-matching similarities plus a hinge forcing margin $m$ between their means.

nodes.name: Gradient of the pairwise similarity global loss $J_2^g$
nodes.statement: The gradient of this global loss function is derived as \begin{equation} \begin{split} \frac{\partial J_2^g}{\partial g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g)} = \frac{2}{N}\big[ & (g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g) -\mu^+)\\&-\frac{1}{2}\mathds{1}((\mu^+ -\mu^-) < m)\big]\\ \frac{\partial J_2^g}{\partial g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g)} = \frac{2}{N}\big[& (g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g) -\mu^-)\\&+\frac{1}{2}\mathds{1}((\mu^+ -\mu^-) < m)\big].\\ \end{split} \end{equation}
conclusions: \begin{split} \frac{\partial J_2^g}{\partial g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g)} = \frac{2}{N}\big[ & (g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^+,\theta_g) -\mu^+)\\&-\frac{1}{2}\mathds{1}((\mu^+ -\mu^-) < m)\big]\\ \frac{\partial J_2^g}{\partial g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g)} = \frac{2}{N}\big[& (g(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_i^-,\theta_g) -\mu^-)\\&+\frac{1}{2}\mathds{1}((\mu^+ -\mu^-) < m)\big].\\ \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form gradients of $J_2^g$ with respect to matching and non-matching similarity scores.

nodes.name: TNet, TLoss
nodes.statement: The {\bf first model} consists of a triplet network trained with the triplet loss in (\ref{eq:loss_triplet_embedding}), which produces an embedding - this is labelled as {\bf TNet, TLoss}.
differentia: trained with the triplet loss in (\ref{eq:loss_triplet_embedding})

nodes.name: TNet, TGLoss
nodes.statement: The {\bf second model} is a triplet network that also produces an embedding and uses the following loss function that combines the original triplet loss (\ref{eq:loss_triplet_embedding}) and the proposed global loss (\ref{eq:loss_global}) for the learning process: \begin{equation} \begin{split} &J_1^{tg}( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N , \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N ) = \\ & \gamma \sum_j J_1^t ( \mathbf{x}_j,\mathbf{x}_j^+, \mathbf{x}_j^-) + J_1^g( \{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i=1}^N , \{ \mathbf{x}_i^+ \}_{i=1}^N, \{ \mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N ),\\ \end{split} \end{equation} -- this model is labelled as {\bf TNet, TGLoss}.
nodes.statement_short: Triplet network trained with the triplet loss plus the global embedding loss.

nodes.name: SNet, GLoss
nodes.statement: The {\bf third model} is a siamese network that produces a similarity estimation of an input pair of local patches, but the model is trained with the siamese global loss defined in (\ref{eq:loss_global_siamese}) -- this model is labelled as {\bf SNet, GLoss}.
differentia: trained with the siamese global loss defined in (\ref{eq:loss_global_siamese})

nodes.name: CS SNet, GLoss
nodes.statement: Finally, the {\bf fourth model} is the central-surround siamese network model described in Sec.~\ref{sec:network_architecture} that also produces the pairwise similarity estimator of an input pair of local patches and is trained with the global loss (\ref{eq:loss_global_siamese}) -- this model is labelled as {\bf CS SNet, GLoss}.
differentia: is trained with the global loss (\ref{eq:loss_global_siamese})

nodes.name: Global loss is robust to outliers (toy problem)
nodes.statement: The label map in Fig.~\ref{fig_toy}-(d) generated by the embedding that uses global loss is coherent even at the locations, where outliers can be found in the training set, indicating that the global loss function is robust to outliers.
conclusions: the global loss function is robust to outliers
nodes.statement_short: On a 2-D toy set with flipped labels, the global-loss embedding yields a coherent nearest-neighbour label map.

nodes.name: False positive rate at 95% recall (FPR95)
nodes.statement: Each model is assessed using the false positive at $95\%$ recall (FPR95) on each of the six combinations of training and testing sets, the mean over all combinations, and the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve also for each of the six combinations.

nodes.name: TNet-TGLoss gives the best embedding result
nodes.statement: From the results in Tab.~\ref{tbl:table_fpr_embedding} and Fig.~\ref{fig:rocall}, we observe that the proposed triplet network trained with a combination of the triplet and global losses (\ie, the {TNet-TGLoss}) shows the best result in the field in terms of feature embedding.
conclusions: the proposed triplet network trained with a combination of the triplet and global losses (\ie, the {TNet-TGLoss}) shows the best result in the field in terms of feature embedding

nodes.name: CS SNet, GLoss halves the state-of-the-art pairwise error
nodes.statement: The pairwise similarity results in Tab.~\ref{tbl:table_fpr_pairwise} and Fig.~\ref{fig:rocall} indicate that our centre-surround siamese network trained with global loss (\ie, the {CS SNet, GLoss}) produces a result that is almost half of the previous state-of-the-art result, \ie, the 2ch-2stream~\cite{ZagoruykoCVPR15}.
conclusions: produces a result that is almost half of the previous state-of-the-art result

nodes.name: Inference cost of embeddings versus siamese similarity networks
nodes.statement: Similar to~\cite{ZagoruykoCVPR15}, we notice that the siamese networks trained with the pairwise similarity loss achieve better classification performance compared to the feature embeddings produced by the triplet loss, but the dependence of the siamese networks on pairwise inputs is a potential issue during inference in terms of complexity. For instance, the $\ell_2$ distance norm computation between feature embeddings can be significantly simplified to a cosine distance dot product, since the descriptor norms are equal to 1, while the siamese networks have to measure the similarity using the final fully connected (FC) layer of the network (assuming the features before that FC layer have been pre-computed).
nodes.statement_short: Siamese similarity nets score better, but unit-norm embeddings allow cheap $\ell_2$/cosine comparison at inference.

nodes.name: TNet-TGLoss beats some pairwise similarity networks
nodes.statement: Even though pairwise similarity methods tend to perform better than feature embedding approaches, according to our results and also the results from~\cite{ZagoruykoCVPR15}, it is interesting to notice that our feature embedding model {TNet-TGLoss} performs better than Siam network~\cite{ZagoruykoCVPR15} and the 512d-F(512) network~\cite{Han_cvpr15}, with both representing examples of pairwise similarity methods.
conclusions: our feature embedding model {TNet-TGLoss} performs better than Siam network~\cite{ZagoruykoCVPR15} and the 512d-F(512) network~\cite{Han_cvpr15}
